title: What Did We MESHA?
author: Greg Ashman
summary: Greg Ashman describes the MESHA Project, a curriculum-referenced assessment he has built with edtech company Edrolo to let Australian schools compare their students' performance question-by-question against a national cohort, rather than relying on vague overall grades. The piece argues that question-level data is uniquely useful because it exposes exactly which misconceptions are driving wrong answers -- for instance, students who pick a specific wrong option on an algebra question because they failed to apply the distributive law -- turning a diagnostic exercise into a precise instructional target. Ashman reports early results from mathematics assessments across Years 7-10 (over 7,000 students in Victoria) and a Year 8 science pilot (707 students), noting that physics items scored lower than biology and chemistry largely because of question difficulty rather than any deep curricular gap. He frames the whole project as an application of Zig Engelmann's dictum that effective instruction is built from attention to many small, specific details rather than sweeping thematic goals, and closes by pointing to schools that have already used MESHA data to fix narrow, identifiable problems like over-reliance on formula sheets.
points: MESHA's core innovation is releasing the actual test questions to schools rather than just aggregate scores, so a school scoring near the cohort average on a specific item can still see it's a 'relatively easy gain' opportunity if the cohort average itself is high.

Wrong-answer distributions function as built-in misconception diagnostics -- a cluster of students choosing one specific distractor on the algebra question reveals a specific unlearned rule (the distributive law), giving teachers a target more actionable than a raw score.

The project deliberately resists giving vague thematic feedback like 'work on forces'; it insists on naming the exact question, which Ashman ties explicitly to Engelmann's philosophy that instruction is fundamentally about accumulating precise, small details rather than big themes.

Real schools are already converting MESHA data into narrow curricular fixes -- one added instruction on teaching the median, another identified and addressed over-reliance on formula sheets -- demonstrating the diagnostic-to-action pipeline the project is designed to enable.
quotes: It is this question-level analysis that is the most powerful feature of MESHA -- and the biggest pain for Edrolo and me because we have to keep writing new questions. It functions as an assessment of the taught curriculum rather than an assessment of individual students.

Your students score similarly to students in other schools on many questions, but the average across the cohort on this question is closer to 70%. Does this mean you should hang your head in shame? No. This is really good news.

Also notice that the wrong answers demonstrate key misconceptions. If many of your students pick B, for example, that tells you they are not applying the distributive law. So now you know what it is you need to teach.

If you find this focus on small details underwhelming, then it's worth remembering the words of the great Zig Engelmann: "There is no big thing. It's all pick, pick, picky details. Direct Instruction is just attention to a lot of tiny details.

Critically, MESHA does not make vague claims about areas to focus on. If we did, we would probably report to schools that they need to 'work on forces'. Instead, it provides the exact question that was asked so that teachers can reverse engineer what is needed -- the picky details.

Schools are already using the data to identify specific, resolvable issues, such as a school that has added to the way it teaches the median and a school that identified that its students were too reliant on formula sheets.
